In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
note: F6 (a): the 12-mark command word on this paper is Evaluate, not Discuss

expect: 12 marks — Discuss a Statement
value: 12 marks — Evaluate a Statement
note: F6 (b): command word

expect: Arguments in support (more alike): Both frameworks share the three central convictions of Tawhid (oneness of Allah), Nubuwwah (prophethood, including Muhammad as the final prophet) and belief in judgement/resurrection. Both ground these convictions in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. The shared emphasis on Tawhid means that in daily worship, prayer and ethical life, Sunni and Shi'a Muslims are largely indistinguishable. A Muslim who accepts the Six Beliefs effectively accepts four of the Five Roots without alteration. Arguments against (more different): The two frameworks diverge on foundational questions. Shi'a Islam replaces al-Qadr with Adl — this is not a minor variation but a theological commitment to Divine Justice that shapes how Shi'a Muslims understand human freedom and moral accountability. Imamah is even more distinctive: it introduces the concept of divinely guided Imams from the Prophet's family (Ahl-ul-Bayt), which has no equivalent in the Sunni six-article framework. For Shi'a Muslims, especially Twelvers, belief in the Hidden Imam and the expectation of his return are central to religious identity in ways the Six Beliefs do not capture. The Sevener/Twelver split further diversifies Shi'a belief. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might note that the two frameworks share more at the level of doctrine about God and revelation than they do at the level of religious authority. Tawhid is identical; what divides the traditions most is Imamah — a belief about who leads the community, not a belief about the nature of God. This suggests the statement is broadly true about God-belief but misleading about the institutional and political dimensions of faith. Mastering (10-12): both sides developed with named sources; weighs perspectives; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides present, one source, conclusion present. Developing (4-6): one side dominant, sources vague. Emerging (1-3): brief, one-sided, no sources.

expect: Arguments in support: The Qur'an is the direct, final and perfectly preserved word of Allah, revealed to Muhammad through Jibril. Surah 5:43-48 describes it as the guardian and confirmation of all earlier scriptures. Unlike the Tawrat, Zabur and Injil, the Qur'an has not been altered by human hands — Muslims believe it remains exactly as revealed. It is recited in prayer five times daily, memorised by millions, and governs Islamic law (Shari'ah). No other source can claim the same direct divine authority. Arguments against: The Sunnah (the Prophet's example, recorded in the Hadith collections including Sahih al-Bukhari) is considered essential for interpreting the Qur'an. Without the Hadith, many Qur'anic commands would be impossible to apply in practice — for example, the Qur'an instructs Muslims to pray but does not specify the exact movements; those come from the Sunnah. For Shi'a Muslims, the authority of the Imam also carries significant weight in interpreting revelation. The Qur'an itself states that Muhammad was sent to explain its teachings to humanity (Surah 16:44), suggesting the Sunnah is integral rather than secondary. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might note that the Qur'an is the highest source in theory — its status as the uncreated word of Allah is undisputed — but in practice Muslims cannot fully live by the Qur'an without the Sunnah as an interpretive guide. The two together form the primary sources of Islamic authority. Mastering (10-12): both sides developed with named Qur'anic anchors; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides present; one source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant; vague sources. Emerging (1-3): brief and one-sided.

expect: Arguments in support: Akhirah gives meaning to every aspect of Muslim life. If there is no judgement, there is no ultimate basis for ethics — why act justly if injustice goes unpunished? The Qur'an repeatedly connects moral commands to the reality of the Day of Judgement, suggesting that the afterlife is the engine of Islamic ethics. Surah 17:49-72 asserts that resurrection is as certain as the first act of creation. For millions of Muslims, the awareness of being watched and recorded gives daily life its moral seriousness. Arguments against: Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is arguably more foundational. Before any question of afterlife arises, a Muslim must believe that there is one God who created, sustains and judges. Without Tawhid, there is no framework within which Akhirah makes sense. Moreover, the Five Pillars (the practical obligations of Islam) are not primarily about preparing for death — they are about continuous submission to Allah in this life: through Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (daily prayer), Zakah (charity), Sawm (fasting) and Hajj (pilgrimage). Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that Tawhid is logically prior to Akhirah — without belief in one just God, the concept of a Day of Judgement has no force. But in terms of day-to-day impact on Muslim behaviour, belief in Akhirah is exceptionally powerful. The statement is defensible but not the only tenable position. Mastering (10-12): both sides with Qur'anic anchors; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant; vague. Emerging (1-3): brief and one-sided.

expect: Arguments in support: Each pillar addresses a different but essential dimension of Muslim faith and practice. Shahadah establishes identity; Salah maintains daily contact with God; Zakah expresses social responsibility; Sawm builds spiritual discipline; Hajj connects the believer to Islamic origins and the global ummah. Neglecting any one weakens the others — as the Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari suggests, Islam is built on all five. Together they form an integrated structure, not a hierarchy. Arguments against: The Shahadah is often described as the most fundamental, since it is the act of becoming Muslim and is embedded within every other pillar. Without affirming the oneness of Allah and the prophethood of Muhammad, the other four pillars are meaningless. Some scholars prioritise Salah as the pillar that is most regularly practised and that most consistently shapes Muslim identity. Hajj is the only pillar many Muslims never perform (due to financial or health constraints), and exemptions exist for Sawm — suggesting these are contextually flexible in ways Salah and Zakah are not. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that the Shahadah is logically primary (it defines what it means to be Muslim) but that in terms of daily impact, Salah is the most shaping practice. The pillars are interdependent rather than strictly equal in weight — their importance varies by context and by individual circumstance. Mastering (10-12): both sides with named sources (Sahih al-Bukhari, Surah references); weighing explicit; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; one source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant. Emerging (1-3): brief and one-sided.

expect: Id-ul-Adha commemorates Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to Allah. It coincides with the end of the Hajj pilgrimage. Muslims sacrifice an animal (qurbani) and share the meat with family, friends and the poor. It involves communal prayer and is one of the two major Islamic festivals. Three descriptive points earn three marks.
value: First reason: Id-ul-Adha remembers Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to Allah (Surah 37:77-111), so it calls Muslims to the same trust and submission. Second reason: the festival turns that obedience into practical charity. Families sacrifice an animal (qurbani) and share the meat with relatives, neighbours and the poor, which strengthens the whole community. Two developed points, two marks each.
note: F23 (c): answer rewritten for the 4-mark Explain two form

expect: First reason: Greater jihad is central to personal spiritual development. Every act of worship — prayer, fasting, charity — requires overcoming the lower self (nafs). Without this inner struggle, outward religious practice can become hollow habit. The Qur'an commands believers to strive for God: Surah 22:39 describes the striving of those who have been wronged, but the broader context of the surah is that striving for God encompasses all dimensions of life. Second reason: Greater jihad is the most continuous form of jihad, lasting from birth to death. It cannot be completed and set aside. This makes it, in classical Islamic scholarship, the greater of the two forms. Greater jihad (the inner struggle against nafs) is considered by classical scholars to be the more important form. Surah 2:190-194 places strict conditions on lesser jihad, making it a constrained, last-resort defence — not an open call to violence. Media and political discourse has reduced a rich theological concept to a single-dimensional caricature of violence. Many Muslims — scholars and practitioners alike — argue that this misrepresentation harms both the religion and wider social understanding. Arguments against: While the inner-struggle interpretation is important, it would also be wrong to suggest that lesser jihad (outward struggle) is not a genuine part of Islamic teaching. The Qur'an does address defensive warfare directly in Surah 2:190-194 and Surah 22:39. Some Islamic scholars throughout history have emphasised outward jihad in specific historical and political contexts. The statement risks overcorrecting — portraying jihad as purely spiritual and ignoring its legitimate outward dimensions. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that most people have misunderstood jihad by reducing it exclusively to violence, since this ignores the greater jihad and the strict conditions on lesser jihad. However, the statement is slightly too absolute — jihad does include an outward dimension that is genuinely part of Islamic teaching, not an invention of misreaders. The fullest understanding acknowledges both dimensions in their proper relationship. Key features include the mihrab (prayer niche indicating Makkah), minbar (pulpit for Friday sermons) and minaret (tower for the call to prayer). value: First way: the mosque is the place of congregational prayer, above all the Friday Jummah prayer. It hosts Qur'an classes, Id celebrations and social events, so it shapes Muslim identity well beyond prayer. Two developed points, two marks each.

expect: Arguments in support: Sufism seeks the inward, spiritual heart of Islamic practice — the direct experience of Allah that makes outward religious duties meaningful. Al-Ghazali, in his Revival of the Religious Sciences, argued that Sufism was not in tension with orthodox Islam but was its deepest fulfilment. Sufis emphasise Surah 13:28 — 'in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest' — as the goal of all religious practice. Rabi'a al-Adawiyya taught that love of Allah, free from any desire for reward, is the purest form of faith. Without this inward dimension, Sufis argue, religious practice risks becoming empty ritual. Arguments against: Many mainstream Sunni and Shi'a scholars have questioned aspects of Sufism. Ibn al-Arabi's concept of the Unity of Being (wahdat al-wujud) has been criticised as blurring the distinction between Allah and creation, which some scholars regard as incompatible with Tawhid. Some Muslim communities have rejected Sufi practices (music, dance, veneration of saints) on the grounds that they introduce innovations (bid'ah) not supported by the Qur'an or Hadith. From this perspective, the Qur'an and Sunnah — not mystical experience — are the authoritative guides to correct Islamic practice. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might note that Sufism has a long and respected history within mainstream Islam, including the endorsement of al-Ghazali, who was himself a respected orthodox scholar. However, describing it as the 'truest' form is contested — other Muslims regard strict adherence to the Qur'an and Sunnah without mystical additions as equally or more authentic. The statement overstates Sufism's claim by suggesting it supersedes other forms of Islamic practice. Developing (4-6): one side dominant. Emerging (1-3): brief.
